Just over 60% of students answered part 1 correctly. In part 2 many students lost this mark by not identifying the electron pair/lone pair was donated from oxygen to copper. Many incorrect observations were seen in part 3. The students who started with CO32– usually gave a correct equation; ions with incorrect formula CO3– were common. In part 4 most students gave the correct shapes; the most common error was square planar instead of tetrahedral. Some students did not refer to ligand size and instead gave ideas based on electron pair repulsion theory; some referred to chlorine atoms/molecules rather than chloride ions. Some students did not refer to d orbital splitting.
Many students referred to light being absorbed but did not identify the light as visible or white. Many students knew that the colour seen was light that had not been absorbed. Few students were able to write about the energy gap and what was responsible for the change in the energy gap, although some did reference the equation ∆E = h𝜈𝜈. Fewer than 20% scored both marks in part 5. Many students gave an incorrect observation. Students found the equation challenging; chlorine was often given as a product, some students had 2 mol of ammonia and 4 mol of water instead of the other way round and the copper complex often lacked a charge.
In part 6 many students could not give a balanced equation; H+ ions were often omitted from the left-hand side and water from the right-hand side. In part 7 most students gave the correct answer; a common error was to average three of the four titres instead of the two that were concordant. The calculation in part 7 proved challenging; most students were able to score the first three marks but then failed to divide by 2 and were not able to make progress. Some students used 25.0 cm3 for their titre. Students who had calculated an Mr greater than 275 usually divided this by 2 to get an Ar but often did not assign this to a metal with a +1 oxidation state. Students found part 9 challenging; common errors were to have a 4- coordinate copper or to bond the copper to a C2O42– ion via 1 coordinate bond. Many students did not specifically draw the coordinate bonds originating from the O atom of the water.

erText: 1.2 Students had to complete a radical substitution mechanism. Many did it well but few used the skeletal formulae expected. The most common error was to use molecular formulae which are ambiguous in terms of the position of substitution.

text:
Hexanedioic acid is an important compound used in organic synthesis.
Hexanedioic acid can be prepared from cyclohexanol.
The equation for the reaction is
C6H11OH(l)  +  2 HNO3(aq)  ⟶  HOOC(CH2)4COOH(s)  +  N2O(g)  +  2 H2O(l)
Method
Step 1 Add 5 cm3 of concentrated nitric acid to a boiling tube.
Step 2 Place the boiling tube in a beaker of water at 85 °C
Step 3 Add 2 cm3 of cyclohexanol dropwise to the boiling tube.
Step 4 Leave the reaction mixture for 10 minutes.
Step 5 Cool the boiling tube in a beaker of cold water for a further 10 minutes.
Step 6 Filter the contents of the boiling tube and collect the impure solid.
Step 7 Recrystallise the impure solid using methanol.
Step 8 Wash the purified crystalline product with some
ice-cold distilled water, and dry.
Step 9 Measure the melting point of the hexanedioic acid.
Suggest why the apparatus should be set up in a fume cupboard.
[1 mark]

erText: 4.1 Students showed good understanding of risk assessment here by identifying reasons for carrying out the method in a fume cupboard .

msText: 04.5 Mistake: Water is being used to warm sample Problem caused: Temperature will not reach high enough (to melt sample) Mistake: Sample is much higher than bottom of thermometer Problem caused: Temperature of sample will be lower / different than reading on the thermometer Mistake: no stirrer is in the boiling tube or boiling tube used instead of D-tube / Thiele tube Problem caused: variation in temperature 4 (4 x AO3)
erText: 4.5 Students were given a diagram of a flawed method used to determine a melting point. Many were able to see that the sample and thermometer bulb were not at the same level so the thermometer temperature reading would be different from the temperature of the sample. Far fewer noted that water boils at a temperature below that of the solid and should be replaced by oil. Some showed good knowledge of the improvement a D tube (Thiele tube) would make in place of the boiling tube given. Common errors suggested by students included those who said that the thermometer should be in the melting point tube, or that the rubber ring would melt or prevent the thermometer reading being taken. Others said that a bung should be added to the boiling tube.

msText: 04.6 Reason process is more sustainable: Any one from • Glucose is a renewable resource / feedstock • Biological reactant / E. coli bacteria is renewable • Pt catalyst can be re-used • Higher atom economy Reason process is less sustainable: Any one from • Synthesis is a 2-stage process • Hydrogen gas is a non-renewable • High pressures (are required in Stage 2) • Uses a Pt catalyst that has been mined from the earth 2 (2 x AO3)
erText: 4.6 Students were shown details of an alternative two stage synthesis of the product and asked to justify it being more or less sustainable. Many observed that biological/natural sources were used but did not state that these are renewable to justify the process as more sustainable. The use of energy from fossil fuels to achieve high pressures was the most common answer given credit as a justification for the process being less sustainable. Large numbers focused on the temperature used but this was almost identical to the temperature used in the original method outlined at the start of the question.

erText: 3.4 There were many confused answers here with many students not paying enough attention to the information given in the stem of the question. The stem describes that iron filings are reacted with copper(II) sulfate, which should point students to their equation needing to start with Fe(s) and Cu2+(aq) as the reactants. Table 4 provided the data for this question and included 2 half-equations containing 3 different iron species and 3 equations containing 3 different copper species. Students therefore need to be very specific about which half-equations they are referring to and this is best done by referring, as on the mark scheme, to the fact that the electrode potential for the Fe3+/Fe2+ electrode is more negative than that for the Cu2+/Cu electrode. Overall the question discriminated very well with close to 30% of students achieving at least 4/6.

mistakes: Levels of response, three stages. Oxidation: acidified potassium dichromate(VI)
CH3CH2CH2OH + [O] → CH3CH2CHO + H2O
CH3CH(OH)CH3 + [O] → CH3COCH3 + H2O (structural, not molecular, formulas). Test: Fehling's solution or Tollens' reagent on both distillates

text:
This question is about oxidation.
A student has separate unlabelled samples of propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol but does
not know which sample is which alcohol.
The student plans a series of steps to identify the alcohols.
Step 1  Oxidise each sample, distilling off the organic product as it is formed.
Step 2  Identify the organic products using a simple chemical test.
Step 3  Confirm the identities using the infrared spectrum of each original sample.
Give further details of each step in the plan.  In your answer include
• an appropriate oxidising agent used in Step 1
• equations, using [O] to represent the oxidising agent, for each reaction in Step 1
• a suitable test and expected observations in Step 2
• how the infrared spectra can be used to confirm the identities.
[6 marks]
msText: 05.1 This question is marked using Levels of Response. Refer to the Scheme Instructions for Examiners for guidance. Level 3 5–6 marks All stages are covered and the explanation of each stage is correct and virtually complete Answer communicates the whole explanation, including equations, coherently and shows a logical progression through all three stages. Level 2 3–4 marks All stages are covered but the explanation of each stage may be incomplete or may contain inaccuracies. OR two stages covered and the explanations are generally correct and virtually complete. Answer is coherent and shows some progression through all three stages. Some steps in each stage may be incomplete. Level 1 1–2 marks Two stages are covered but the explanation of each stage may be incomplete or may contain inaccuracies. OR only one stage is covered but the explanation is generally correct and virtually complete. Answer shows some progression between two stages. 0 mark Insufficient correct chemistry to gain a mark. Stage 1: Oxidation of the alcohols (covered = 1/3; virtually complete = 2/3) 1a – use acidified potassium dichromate(VI) to oxidise both samples 1b – CH3CH2CH2OH + [O] → CH3CH2CHO + H2O 1c – CH3CH(OH)CH3 + [O] → CH3COCH3 + H2O NOT molecular formulae Stage 2: Testing the aldehyde/ketone formed by the oxidation (covered = 1/3; virtually complete = 2/3) 2a – test both samples using Fehling’s solution / Tollens’ reagent / acidified potassium dichromate(VI) 2b – propanal (or product of oxidation of propan-1-ol) will form brick red precipitate / silver mirror / (orange to) green (solution) 2c – propanone (or product of oxidation of propan-2-ol) will have no visible change / no reaction Stage 3: Use of IR spectroscopy (covered = 1/3; virtually complete = 2/3) 3a – Both show absorption at 3230-3550 (for O–H alcohol) 3b – use the fingerprint region of each sample 3c – find an (exact) match to a database / idea that fingerprint region is unique to an individual compound 6 (6 x AO3)
erText: 5.1 This is the Levels of Response question and almost 25% of students were able to access level 3 while around 65% accessed Level 2 or above. Students were strong on stage 2, with most including all three pieces of indicative content in that stage. However, in stage 1 many students found it tricky to produce properly balanced equations for oxidation of the alcohols with [O] and many forgot water as the second product. In stage 3, as mentioned above, many students failed to read the question carefully enough and produced an answer that discussed the IR spectra of the carbonyls instead of the IR spectra of the original alcohols. 3b and 3c were still accessible in such cases for a clear description of how to use the fingerprint region.
